title: D3.3 Homeostasis
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: D3.3 Homeostasis — IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025), topic D3.3.
meta_desc: IB DP Biology practice covering D3.3 Homeostasis, guide topic D3.3.
final_note: You worked through D3.3 Homeostasis — 11 guide statements.

concepts.def: The maintenance of the internal environment of an organism, in which variables such as body temperature, blood pH, blood glucose concentration and blood osmotic concentration are kept within preset limits despite fluctuations in the external environment. The variable is not held at one fixed value: it oscillates within a narrow range around a set point.

The set point is the value of a homeostatic variable that the control system works to restore, such as a core body temperature of about 37 °C, a blood pH of about 7.4, a blood glucose concentration of about 4–6 mmol L−1 between meals and a blood osmotic concentration of about 0.3 osmol L−1. The preset limits are the narrow range either side of the set point within which the variable is allowed to fluctuate before corrective responses become strong.

A control mechanism in which a change in a variable away from its set point triggers responses that reverse the change, returning the variable towards the set point. It operates in both directions: a value above the set point is brought down and a value below is brought up. Negative feedback is used in homeostasis because it is self-correcting and stabilizing.

A control mechanism in which a change in a variable triggers responses that increase the change further, driving the variable away from its starting value until some end point is reached. Positive feedback amplifies deviations rather than correcting them, so it is unsuitable for homeostasis; it is used where a rapid, one-way completion is needed, such as the oxytocin-driven contractions of childbirth.

A peptide hormone secreted by the beta cells of the pancreatic islets when blood glucose concentration rises above the set point, for example after a meal. It is transported dissolved in the blood plasma to all tissues but acts only on cells with insulin receptors. In its target cells it increases the uptake of glucose from the blood, stimulates the conversion of glucose to glycogen in liver and skeletal muscle cells, and increases the use of glucose in cell respiration, so blood glucose concentration falls.

A peptide hormone secreted by the alpha cells of the pancreatic islets when blood glucose concentration falls below the set point, for example during fasting or exercise. Carried in the blood plasma, it acts on liver cells, stimulating the breakdown of stored glycogen to glucose and the release of that glucose into the blood, so blood glucose concentration rises.

concepts.term: Pancreatic endocrine cells (islet alpha and beta cells)
concepts.def: Clusters of hormone-secreting cells in the pancreas, the islets of Langerhans, that monitor blood glucose concentration directly. Beta cells secrete insulin in response to high glucose and alpha cells secrete glucagon in response to low glucose; each hormone is released into the blood, not into a duct, which is what makes these cells endocrine. The two hormones are antagonistic, so together they return blood glucose to the set point from above and from below.

A branched polysaccharide of glucose stored as granules in liver and skeletal muscle cells. Insulin stimulates its synthesis from glucose when blood glucose is high; glucagon stimulates its breakdown to glucose in the liver when blood glucose is low. Glycogen is the short-term glucose store, not to be confused with glucagon, the hormone.

A form of diabetes in which the beta cells of the pancreatic islets are destroyed by the person's own immune system (an autoimmune disease), so little or no insulin is secreted and blood glucose concentration rises to dangerously high values after meals. It usually develops in childhood or adolescence; the main risk factor is a genetic predisposition and it cannot be prevented by lifestyle. It is treated by regular injections or pump delivery of insulin, timed and dosed against food intake and blood glucose testing.

A form of diabetes in which insulin is still secreted, at least at first, but the target cells no longer respond to it normally (insulin resistance) because of changes in their receptors and signalling, so glucose is not taken up and blood glucose concentration stays high. Beta-cell output may decline later. Risk factors are obesity, especially abdominal fat, diets rich in sugar and fat, physical inactivity, increasing age and family history. It can be largely prevented, and initially treated, by diet and exercise; drugs that increase insulin sensitivity or secretion are added when needed, and some patients eventually need insulin.

Sensory receptors in the skin that detect the temperature of the skin and of the external environment and send nerve impulses to the hypothalamus. They provide an early warning of heat loss or gain before the core temperature changes. The hypothalamus also contains central thermoreceptors that monitor the temperature of the blood flowing through it.

The part of the brain that acts as the control centre for body temperature. It compares the temperature of the blood passing through it, and the input from peripheral thermoreceptors, with the set point of about 37 °C, then coordinates responses: nerve impulses to effectors such as skeletal muscle, arteriole smooth muscle, sweat glands and arrector pili muscles, and hormonal signals via the pituitary gland.

A hormone secreted by the thyroid gland that raises the metabolic rate of most body cells, increasing the rate of cell respiration and so the amount of heat released. Its secretion is stimulated by thyroid-stimulating hormone from the pituitary gland, which is in turn controlled by the hypothalamus. Thyroxin release rises in prolonged cold exposure, providing a slower, longer-lasting increase in heat generation than the rapid nervous responses.

Birds and mammals regulate their body temperature by physiological means (the effector tissues below) and by behavioural means such as seeking shade, sun or shelter; the guide requires the details only for humans. The tissues that carry out thermoregulatory responses. Muscle effectors include skeletal muscle (shivering), smooth muscle in the walls of skin arterioles (vasoconstriction and vasodilation) and the arrector pili muscles (hair erection). Adipose tissue effectors include brown adipose tissue, which generates heat by uncoupled respiration; white adipose tissue insulates. Sweat glands are the effector for evaporative cooling.

Changes in the diameter of the arterioles supplying capillaries near the skin surface, brought about by smooth muscle in the arteriole walls. Vasodilation widens the arterioles so more warm blood flows through the surface capillaries and more heat is lost by radiation, conduction and convection. Vasoconstriction narrows them so less blood reaches the surface and heat is retained in the core. The capillaries themselves do not move and cannot constrict.

Rapid, involuntary, rhythmic contractions of skeletal muscle triggered by the hypothalamus when the body is cold. The contractions do little useful work, so most of the energy released by the increased cell respiration in the muscle fibres is released as heat, which warms the blood passing through the muscle.

Secretion of sweat, a dilute salt solution, onto the skin surface by sweat glands when the body is too hot. Cooling occurs only when the water in the sweat evaporates, because evaporation absorbs latent heat from the skin; sweat that drips off without evaporating removes very little heat, which is why sweating is less effective in humid air.

concepts.term: Uncoupled respiration in brown adipose tissue
concepts.def: Heat generation in brown adipose tissue, found especially in infants and around the neck and shoulders of adults. Its mitochondria contain an uncoupling protein in the inner membrane that lets protons flow back into the matrix without passing through ATP synthase, so the energy of the proton gradient built by the electron transport chain is released as heat instead of being used to make ATP. The tissue is brown because of its very many mitochondria and rich blood supply.

Contraction of the arrector pili muscles attached to hair follicles, pulling the hairs upright when the body is cold. In furred mammals the raised hairs trap a thicker layer of still air next to the skin, reducing heat loss; in humans the hair is too sparse for this to insulate effectively, and the response persists as 'goose bumps'.

The removal from the body of the waste products of metabolism, such as urea from the breakdown of excess amino acids and carbon dioxide from cell respiration, together with other toxic or unwanted solutes. The kidneys excrete urea and other solutes in urine. Excretion is distinct from egestion, the elimination of undigested food that was never part of the body's metabolism.

The regulation of the osmotic concentration of the blood and other body fluids, achieved in humans mainly by the kidneys adjusting how much water is reabsorbed from the filtrate and therefore the volume and concentration of the urine. Osmoregulation and excretion are separate roles of the kidney: one controls water balance, the other removes metabolic waste.

The total concentration of osmotically active solute particles in a solution, measured in osmoles per litre (osmol L−1); a solute that dissociates into two ions contributes two osmoles per mole. Human blood plasma is kept at about 0.3 osmol L−1 (300 mosmol L−1). Water moves by osmosis from a solution of lower osmotic concentration to one of higher osmotic concentration.

Filtration of blood plasma under pressure in the glomerulus, a knot of capillaries inside Bowman's capsule. High blood pressure in the glomerular capillaries, caused by the efferent arteriole being narrower than the afferent arteriole, forces water and small solutes (glucose, amino acids, salts, urea) through the fenestrated capillary wall, the basement membrane and the slits between podocytes into Bowman's capsule. Blood cells and plasma proteins are too large to pass, so the filtrate is plasma minus its proteins.

concepts.term: Selective reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule
concepts.def: The recovery of useful substances from the glomerular filtrate back into the blood in the proximal convoluted tubule. All of the glucose and amino acids and most of the sodium ions are reabsorbed by active transport through the tubule cells, and water follows by osmosis, so about 80% of the filtrate volume is returned. Urea and other toxins are not actively reabsorbed and so remain in the filtrate to be excreted in urine. The tubule cells have microvilli and many mitochondria for this task.

The hairpin-shaped section of the nephron that dips from the cortex into the medulla and back. Cells of the ascending limb actively transport sodium ions out of the filtrate into the medullary interstitial fluid, and the ascending limb is impermeable to water, so the medulla is kept at a high osmotic concentration that increases with depth. This high concentration is what allows water to be drawn by osmosis out of the collecting ducts, which pass down through the medulla, when aquaporins are present.

A peptide hormone produced by neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary gland when osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect a rise in blood osmotic concentration. ADH acts on the cells of the collecting ducts, increasing their permeability to water so that more water is reabsorbed into the medulla and blood; the urine becomes smaller in volume and more concentrated. When blood osmotic concentration falls, ADH secretion falls and dilute urine is produced.

Cells in the hypothalamus that monitor the osmotic concentration of the blood, shrinking when the blood becomes more concentrated. Their signals increase the rate of ADH secretion from the pituitary gland and also produce the sensation of thirst; when the blood is dilute they signal less, ADH secretion falls and water is excreted.

Water channel proteins whose location in collecting duct cells is switched by ADH. When ADH binds to receptors on the duct cells, intracellular vesicles carrying aquaporins fuse with the plasma membrane facing the filtrate, so water can pass by osmosis into the cells and on into the concentrated medulla. When ADH is absent the aquaporins are withdrawn by endocytosis back into vesicles, the membrane becomes almost impermeable to water and dilute urine leaves the duct.

The change in the share of cardiac output sent to different organs as activity changes, brought about by vasodilation of arterioles in organs that need more blood and vasoconstriction in those that need less. During vigorous physical activity skeletal muscles receive the great majority of a much increased cardiac output while flow to the gut and kidneys is sharply reduced; during wakeful rest the gut and kidneys receive large shares; during sleep cardiac output is lower and flow to skeletal muscle is minimal. Blood flow to the brain is held nearly constant in all three states.

mcqs.q: Which statement about homeostasis in humans is correct?
options: Blood glucose concentration fluctuates within narrow preset limits around a set point.
Core body temperature is held at exactly 37 °C with no variation at all.
Skin temperature is kept within preset limits whatever the air temperature.
Blood pH is corrected only when it rises above its set point of about 7.4.
mcqs.specStatementText: What homeostasis keeps steady
mcqs.explain: Homeostasis maintains the internal environment by keeping variables such as blood glucose concentration within preset limits. The value is not fixed: it rises after a meal and falls during fasting, and negative feedback keeps these swings within a narrow range around the set point.
rationales: Homeostasis maintains the internal environment by keeping variables such as blood glucose concentration within preset limits. The value is not fixed: it rises after a meal and falls during fasting, and negative feedback keeps these swings within a narrow range around the set point.

A student who thinks homeostasis means perfect constancy picks this. Core temperature normally varies by a few tenths of a degree through the day; homeostasis keeps it within preset limits, not at one exact value.

A student who confuses the body's surface with its internal environment picks this. Skin temperature is allowed to vary widely; it is core temperature, blood pH, blood glucose and blood osmotic concentration that are the regulated variables.
A student who thinks homeostatic control acts in one direction only picks this. Blood pH is returned to the set point from values above and from values below it.

mcqs.q: A person's core temperature was recorded at intervals through a day on which the air temperature ranged from 5 °C to 30 °C. The readings were 36.6, 36.9, 37.2, 36.8 and 37.1 °C. What do these readings show?
options: Homeostasis has failed, because the core temperature was not held at one constant value through the day.
Core temperature is being kept within preset limits despite large changes in the external environment.
The readings cannot show homeostasis: skin temperature, not the core, is what is kept within limits.
Only the readings above 37 °C were brought back by negative feedback; the lower ones were not.
mcqs.specStatementText: What homeostasis keeps steady
mcqs.explain: The air temperature varied by 25 °C but the core temperature stayed within 0.4 °C of 37 °C (a total range of only 0.6 °C). That is homeostasis: the internal variable fluctuates only within narrow preset limits while the external environment changes far more.
rationales: A student who expects a homeostatic variable to be perfectly constant picks this. Small oscillations around the set point are the normal signature of negative feedback, not evidence of failure.

The air temperature varied by 25 °C but the core temperature stayed within 0.4 °C of 37 °C (a total range of only 0.6 °C). That is homeostasis: the internal variable fluctuates only within narrow preset limits while the external environment changes far more.

A student who takes the regulated variable to be the body's surface rather than its internal environment picks this. Skin temperature is allowed to vary widely; it is the core temperature, along with blood pH, blood glucose and blood osmotic concentration, that is held within preset limits (D3.3.1).

A student who thinks negative feedback corrects only rises picks this. The readings below 37 °C were also followed by a return towards the set point, because negative feedback acts from both directions.

mcqs.q: Why are homeostatic variables controlled by negative feedback rather than by positive feedback?
options: Negative feedback responds to harmful changes, while positive feedback responds to beneficial ones.
Negative feedback lowers a variable that has risen, which is the usual direction of deviation.
Negative feedback opposes a change, returning the variable towards its set point.
Negative feedback keeps the variable fixed at the set point with no fluctuation.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why negative feedback, not positive
mcqs.explain: In negative feedback the response reverses the deviation that triggered it, so the variable is pushed back towards the set point from either side. Positive feedback amplifies a change and would drive the variable ever further away, so it cannot maintain a set point.
rationales: A student who reads 'positive' and 'negative' as value judgements picks this. The words describe the direction of the response relative to the change, not whether the change is good or bad for the organism.
A student who equates 'negative' with 'decrease' picks this. Negative feedback also raises a variable that has fallen; it is defined by opposing the change, not by lowering.

In negative feedback the response reverses the deviation that triggered it, so the variable is pushed back towards the set point from either side. Positive feedback amplifies a change and would drive the variable ever further away, so it cannot maintain a set point.

A student who thinks homeostasis means perfect constancy picks this. Negative feedback produces small oscillations around the set point, because a response is only triggered after a deviation has occurred.

mcqs.q: During a long run, a person's blood glucose concentration falls to 3.5 mmol L−1. Glucagon secretion increases and the concentration returns to 5 mmol L−1. Which description of this sequence is correct?
options: Positive feedback, because the response raised the variable, not lowered it.
Positive feedback, because the response was beneficial and restored health.
A breakdown of homeostasis, because glucose left its set point of 5 mmol L−1.
Negative feedback correcting a fall of the variable below its set point.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why negative feedback, not positive
mcqs.explain: The variable dropped below its set point and the response (glucagon) raised it back. Because the response opposed the change, this is negative feedback; it operates from below the set point just as insulin operates from above it.
rationales: A student who thinks negative feedback can only lower a variable picks this. The direction that matters is relative to the deviation: the fall was reversed, so the feedback is negative.
A student who reads 'positive' as beneficial picks this. Positive feedback means a response that increases the original change; a beneficial correction that reverses a change is negative feedback.

A student who expects a regulated variable to stay fixed picks this. A deviation followed by a corrective return is homeostasis working, not failing; variables must move away from the set point before feedback can act.

The variable dropped below its set point and the response (glucagon) raised it back. Because the response opposed the change, this is negative feedback; it operates from below the set point just as insulin operates from above it.

mcqs.q: Blood glucose concentration rises after a meal. What happens next?
options: Beta cells of the pancreatic islets secrete insulin into the blood, and target cells take up more glucose.
The hypothalamus detects the rise and sends nerve impulses telling the pancreas to release insulin.
Insulin is released into the blood, where it breaks down the excess glucose molecules.
The pancreas secretes glycogen, which stores the excess glucose in the cells of the liver.
mcqs.specStatementText: Insulin and glucagon control blood glucose
mcqs.explain: The beta cells of the pancreatic islets detect the rise directly and secrete insulin into the blood. Insulin is carried in the plasma to target cells, which take up glucose and convert it to glycogen or respire it, so the concentration falls.
rationales: The beta cells of the pancreatic islets detect the rise directly and secrete insulin into the blood. Insulin is carried in the plasma to target cells, which take up glucose and convert it to glycogen or respire it, so the concentration falls.

A student who models every homeostatic loop on thermoregulation picks this. In blood glucose control the beta cells of the pancreatic islets are themselves the sensors and secrete insulin without instructions from the brain.
A student who treats insulin as an enzyme picks this. Insulin is a hormone: it acts on target cells so that glucose leaves the blood by uptake into cells; it does not digest glucose in the plasma.
A student who has merged glycogen and glucagon picks this. Glycogen is the storage polysaccharide made inside liver and muscle cells; the hormone secreted after a meal is insulin.

mcqs.q: Insulin is secreted into the blood, yet only cells such as liver, skeletal muscle and adipose cells respond to it. Why?
options: Insulin is carried by the blood directly to these organs and to no other part of the body.
Insulin reaches every tissue, but only these cells have receptors that bind it.
Insulin breaks down glucose only in tissues where glucose is concentrated.
The hypothalamus directs the insulin only to those organs that need it most.
mcqs.specStatementText: Insulin and glucagon control blood glucose
mcqs.explain: Hormones are transported in the plasma to all parts of the body. Target specificity comes from receptor proteins: cells carrying insulin receptors respond, while cells without them are exposed to the same insulin and are unaffected.
rationales: A student who pictures hormones travelling point-to-point like a nerve impulse picks this. The blood delivers insulin everywhere; there is no directed route to particular organs.

Hormones are transported in the plasma to all parts of the body. Target specificity comes from receptor proteins: cells carrying insulin receptors respond, while cells without them are exposed to the same insulin and are unaffected.
A student who thinks insulin is an enzyme acting on glucose picks this. Insulin acts on cells, not on glucose, and the cells that respond are those with insulin receptors.
A student who inserts a brain control centre into glucose regulation picks this. The hypothalamus plays no part in routing insulin; distribution is by the blood and specificity is by receptors.

mcqs.q: Which option correctly pairs a hormone with its effect on target cells?
options: Glycogen: liver cells release glucose when its concentration in the blood falls too low.
Insulin: enzymes in the blood plasma digest glucose so that its concentration falls.
Glucagon: liver cells hydrolyse glycogen and release glucose into the blood.
Insulin: liver cells alone receive it, as the pancreas sends it there.
mcqs.specStatementText: Insulin and glucagon control blood glucose
mcqs.explain: Glucagon, secreted by alpha cells when blood glucose is low, binds to receptors on liver cells and stimulates the breakdown of stored glycogen to glucose, which is released into the blood to raise its concentration.
rationales: A student who has merged the two similar words picks this. Glycogen is the polysaccharide store inside liver cells, not a hormone; the hormone that triggers its breakdown is glucagon.
A student who thinks insulin works like an enzyme picks this. Insulin's effects are on cells: increased glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis and respiration. Glucose is not digested in the plasma.

Glucagon, secreted by alpha cells when blood glucose is low, binds to receptors on liver cells and stimulates the breakdown of stored glycogen to glucose, which is released into the blood to raise its concentration.

A student who thinks hormones are delivered to one target picks this. Insulin is carried in the blood to all tissues and acts on every cell type with insulin receptors, including muscle and adipose cells.

mcqs.q: What is the physiological change that underlies type 2 diabetes?
options: Beta cells are destroyed by the immune system.
Beta cells are damaged by dietary sugar.
Insulin in the blood stops digesting glucose.
Target cells respond less to insulin.
mcqs.specStatementText: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes
mcqs.explain: In type 2 diabetes insulin is secreted, at least in the early years, but liver, muscle and adipose cells have become insensitive to it, so glucose uptake falls and blood glucose stays high. This insulin resistance is why diet and exercise, which restore sensitivity, are the first treatments.
rationales: A student who files both types of diabetes under 'no insulin' picks this. Autoimmune destruction of beta cells is the basis of type 1; in type 2 the cells are present and insulin is secreted, but its targets respond poorly.

A student who thinks sugar itself injures the pancreas picks this. A sugar-rich diet is a risk factor for type 2 because it contributes to obesity and insulin resistance, not because it destroys beta cells.
A student who treats insulin as an enzyme picks this. Insulin never digests glucose; it signals to cells to take glucose up. In type 2 diabetes the signal is sent but the cells respond weakly.

In type 2 diabetes insulin is secreted, at least in the early years, but liver, muscle and adipose cells have become insensitive to it, so glucose uptake falls and blood glucose stays high. This insulin resistance is why diet and exercise, which restore sensitivity, are the first treatments.

mcqs.q: A lean 12-year-old develops very high blood glucose within a few weeks; antibodies against pancreatic islet cells are found in the blood and blood insulin is very low. A 55-year-old with obesity has had slowly rising fasting blood glucose for years, with a high blood insulin concentration. Which interpretation is best supported?
options: The child has type 1 diabetes from autoimmune loss of beta cells; the adult has type 2, with insulin secreted but target cells resistant to it.
Both have the same disorder, a pancreas that has stopped making insulin, seen at an early and at a late stage of the disease.
The child's diabetes must have been caused by a sugary diet, because it appeared in childhood; the adult's by the ageing of the pancreas.
Both need insulin injections at once, because a high blood glucose concentration shows that insulin is lacking in each case.
mcqs.specStatementText: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes
mcqs.explain: Islet-cell antibodies, rapid onset in childhood and very low insulin point to autoimmune destruction of beta cells (type 1). Years of rising glucose despite high insulin, with obesity, show that insulin is present but its targets are not responding (type 2 insulin resistance).
rationales: Islet-cell antibodies, rapid onset in childhood and very low insulin point to autoimmune destruction of beta cells (type 1). Years of rising glucose despite high insulin, with obesity, show that insulin is present but its targets are not responding (type 2 insulin resistance).
A student who believes all diabetes is an insulin shortage picks this. The adult's blood insulin is high, which rules out a failure to make insulin; the problem is the response of the target cells.
A student who transfers the lifestyle explanation of type 2 onto type 1 picks this. The islet-cell antibodies show an autoimmune cause in the child; diet does not cause type 1 and cannot prevent it.

A student who equates diabetes treatment with insulin injection picks this. The child does need insulin. The adult has plenty of insulin already; the first treatments are weight loss, diet and exercise to restore sensitivity, with drugs added if needed.

mcqs.q: Which change would do most to reduce a middle-aged adult's risk of developing type 2 diabetes?
options: Beginning insulin injections before any symptoms appear.
Reducing body fat through diet and regular physical activity.
Avoiding the viral infections thought to trigger loss of beta cells.
Taking enzyme supplements that digest glucose in the blood.
mcqs.specStatementText: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes
mcqs.explain: Obesity, a diet rich in sugar and fat, and inactivity are the main modifiable risk factors for type 2 diabetes because they reduce the sensitivity of target cells to insulin. Losing fat and exercising restore sensitivity, so this is the prevention the guide expects.
rationales: A student who thinks insulin injection is the answer to any diabetes picks this. Type 2 is a failure of cells to respond to insulin, not a shortage of it; extra insulin does not prevent insulin resistance developing.

Obesity, a diet rich in sugar and fat, and inactivity are the main modifiable risk factors for type 2 diabetes because they reduce the sensitivity of target cells to insulin. Losing fat and exercising restore sensitivity, so this is the prevention the guide expects.
A student who treats both types as the same failure of the pancreas picks this. Autoimmune destruction of beta cells, possibly triggered by infection, underlies type 1, not type 2.
A student who thinks blood glucose is lowered by digesting it picks this. Glucose leaves the blood by uptake into cells under the control of insulin; no enzyme in the plasma removes it.

mcqs.q: What is the role of the hypothalamus in thermoregulation?
options: It passes on the core temperature measured by thermoreceptors in the skin to the effectors.
It generates heat itself whenever the blood flowing through it becomes too cold.
It monitors blood temperature and coordinates the responses of the effectors.
It secretes thyroxin directly into the blood to raise the metabolic rate.
mcqs.specStatementText: Thermoregulation: sensors, control centre, hormone, effectors
mcqs.explain: The hypothalamus contains thermoreceptors that measure the temperature of the blood flowing through it and also receives impulses from peripheral thermoreceptors in the skin. It compares these with the set point and sends nerve impulses to effectors and hormonal signals via the pituitary gland.
rationales: A student who thinks the skin receptors measure the core picks this. Peripheral thermoreceptors detect skin and external temperature; the core temperature is measured by the hypothalamus itself from the blood.
A student who reads 'controls temperature' as 'does the warming' picks this. The hypothalamus is a control centre; heat is generated by effectors such as skeletal muscle and brown adipose tissue.

The hypothalamus contains thermoreceptors that measure the temperature of the blood flowing through it and also receives impulses from peripheral thermoreceptors in the skin. It compares these with the set point and sends nerve impulses to effectors and hormonal signals via the pituitary gland.
A student who has attached thyroxin to the wrong gland picks this. Thyroxin is secreted by the thyroid gland; the hypothalamus acts on the pituitary gland, which stimulates the thyroid.

mcqs.q: A person moves to a cold climate. After several weeks their resting metabolic rate has risen and they produce more heat even when not shivering. Which explanation is correct?
options: The pituitary gland is secreting thyroxin, which acts as quickly as a nerve impulse.
The hypothalamus has started to produce extra heat itself as the blood cools.
A thicker layer of white fat is making extra ATP, and the ATP is released as heat.
More thyroxin is being secreted, raising the rate of cell respiration.
mcqs.specStatementText: Thermoregulation: sensors, control centre, hormone, effectors
mcqs.explain: Prolonged cold exposure increases signalling from the hypothalamus to the pituitary gland, which stimulates the thyroid gland to secrete more thyroxin. Thyroxin raises the metabolic rate of most cells, so more heat is released; this hormonal response builds up over days, unlike shivering.
rationales: A student who has merged the gland sequence and time scale picks this. The pituitary releases thyroid-stimulating hormone; thyroxin comes from the thyroid gland, and its effect on metabolic rate develops over days, not seconds.

A student who thinks the control centre is also the heater picks this. The hypothalamus coordinates responses; the extra heat comes from the raised respiration of body tissues under the influence of thyroxin.

A student who confuses insulating white fat with heat-generating brown fat, and who thinks heat comes from ATP, picks this. White adipose tissue insulates; the raised metabolic rate here comes from thyroxin.

Prolonged cold exposure increases signalling from the hypothalamus to the pituitary gland, which stimulates the thyroid gland to secrete more thyroxin. Thyroxin raises the metabolic rate of most cells, so more heat is released; this hormonal response builds up over days, unlike shivering.

mcqs.q: How does vasodilation of the arterioles in the skin lower body temperature?
options: More blood flows through the capillaries near the surface, so more heat is lost to the air.
The blood vessels move closer to the surface of the skin, so heat escapes more easily.
Warm blood at the surface is cooled by the cold sweat that lies on top of the skin.
The capillaries contract their walls to squeeze warm blood towards the surface.
mcqs.specStatementText: The human responses to hot and cold
mcqs.explain: Relaxation of smooth muscle in the arteriole walls widens them, so a greater volume of warm blood passes through the capillary beds close to the skin surface, where heat is transferred to the surroundings by radiation, conduction and convection.
rationales: Relaxation of smooth muscle in the arteriole walls widens them, so a greater volume of warm blood passes through the capillary beds close to the skin surface, where heat is transferred to the surroundings by radiation, conduction and convection.

A student who reads the 'hot' and 'cold' diagrams literally picks this. Vessels are fixed in position; what changes is the diameter of the arterioles and therefore the flow of blood through the surface capillaries.

A student who thinks sweat is cold picks this. Sweat is secreted at body temperature; it cools the skin only as it evaporates, and vasodilation works independently by delivering more warm blood to the surface.
A student who gives capillaries a muscular wall picks this. Capillaries have no muscle and cannot constrict or squeeze; flow through them is set upstream by the smooth muscle of the arterioles.

mcqs.q: On a hot, very humid day a runner sweats heavily, but their body temperature keeps rising. Why is sweating less effective in these conditions?
options: The sweat produced is warmer than usual, so it cannot chill the skin as it runs off.
Little of the sweat evaporates, so little latent heat is taken from the skin.
Humid air stops the blood vessels from moving up to the surface of the skin.
Sweat cools mainly as it drips off, and humid air makes it drip slowly.
mcqs.specStatementText: The human responses to hot and cold
mcqs.explain: Sweat cools the body only when its water evaporates, absorbing latent heat from the skin. In humid air the rate of evaporation is low, so most sweat drips off unevaporated and removes almost no heat.
rationales: A student who thinks sweat cools by being a cool liquid picks this. Sweat is at body temperature whatever the weather; it is evaporation, not the temperature of the liquid, that removes heat.
Sweat cools the body only when its water evaporates, absorbing latent heat from the skin. In humid air the rate of evaporation is low, so most sweat drips off unevaporated and removes almost no heat.
A student who thinks vessels relocate picks this. Blood vessels do not move, and humidity has no effect on vasodilation; the problem is the low rate of evaporation.

A student who thinks heat leaves in the liquid sweat picks this. Sweat that drips off has removed almost no heat; only the fraction that evaporates cools the skin, and that fraction is small in humid air.

mcqs.q: Brown adipose tissue in a newborn baby releases heat when the baby is cold. Which statement describes the mechanism?
options: The mitochondria make ATP unusually fast, and the ATP is then broken down to release heat.
The tissue forms a thick insulating layer of fat, so heat generated elsewhere in the body is retained.
Protons re-enter the mitochondrial matrix without passing through ATP synthase, releasing heat.
Thyroxin from the hypothalamus stimulates the tissue, raising its metabolic rate within seconds.
mcqs.specStatementText: The human responses to hot and cold
mcqs.explain: An uncoupling protein in the inner mitochondrial membrane of brown adipose cells lets protons flow back into the matrix without driving ATP synthase, so the energy of the proton gradient built by the electron transport chain is released as heat rather than stored in ATP. This is uncoupled respiration.
rationales: A student who cannot picture respiration without ATP as its product picks this. In uncoupled respiration ATP synthase is bypassed; the heat is released directly from the dissipation of the proton gradient, not from ATP hydrolysis.
A student who thinks all fat is insulation picks this. That is the role of white adipose tissue; brown adipose tissue is an active heat generator packed with mitochondria.

An uncoupling protein in the inner mitochondrial membrane of brown adipose cells lets protons flow back into the matrix without driving ATP synthase, so the energy of the proton gradient built by the electron transport chain is released as heat rather than stored in ATP. This is uncoupled respiration.

A student who attaches thyroxin to the wrong gland and the wrong time scale picks this. Thyroxin is secreted by the thyroid gland and changes heat production over days; brown adipose tissue in a cold baby is activated by sympathetic nerve impulses and generates heat by uncoupled respiration in its mitochondria (D3.3.6).

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes osmoregulation from excretion?
options: Osmoregulation removes surplus water; excretion removes surplus solutes of every other kind.
Osmoregulation is carried out by the kidneys; excretion includes egestion of faeces by the gut.
Osmoregulation regulates the concentration of urea; excretion removes water from the body in urine.
Osmoregulation controls blood osmotic concentration; excretion removes metabolic waste.
mcqs.specStatementText: Excretion and osmoregulation are different jobs
mcqs.explain: Osmoregulation is the regulation of the osmotic concentration of the blood (about 0.3 osmol L−1), achieved by adjusting water reabsorption. Excretion is the removal of the waste products of metabolism, such as urea. The kidney does both, but they are separate roles.
rationales: A student who hears 'regulation' as 'removal' picks this. Osmoregulation may conserve water as well as discard it, and excretion concerns metabolic waste products specifically, not every solute.
A student who counts all waste leaving the body as excretion picks this. Faeces are mainly undigested food that never entered metabolism; their removal is egestion, not excretion.
A student who has swapped the two roles picks this. Urea removal is excretion; the regulated variable in osmoregulation is the osmotic concentration of the blood, not urea.

Osmoregulation is the regulation of the osmotic concentration of the blood (about 0.3 osmol L−1), achieved by adjusting water reabsorption. Excretion is the removal of the waste products of metabolism, such as urea. The kidney does both, but they are separate roles.

mcqs.q: Blood plasma has an osmotic concentration of about 0.30 osmol L−1. Red blood cells are placed in a 0.15 mol L−1 solution of sodium chloride, which dissociates fully into ions. What happens to the cells?
options: Nothing visible: the solution is 0.30 osmol L−1, the same as plasma, so there is no net osmosis.
The cells swell, because 0.15 osmol L−1 is half the osmotic concentration of the plasma.
The cells shrink, as water leaves them for the more dilute 0.15 osmol L−1 solution outside.
The cells shrink, because water moves to where there is more water, and the saline has more.
mcqs.specStatementText: Excretion and osmoregulation are different jobs
mcqs.explain: Each mole of NaCl gives two moles of osmotically active particles, so 0.15 mol L−1 NaCl is 0.30 osmol L−1. That equals the osmotic concentration of plasma, so water enters and leaves the cells at equal rates. This is why 0.15 mol L−1 (0.9%) saline is used clinically.
rationales: Each mole of NaCl gives two moles of osmotically active particles, so 0.15 mol L−1 NaCl is 0.30 osmol L−1. That equals the osmotic concentration of plasma, so water enters and leaves the cells at equal rates. This is why 0.15 mol L−1 (0.9%) saline is used clinically.
A student who equates osmotic concentration with molar concentration picks this. NaCl dissociates into two ions per formula unit, so the osmotic concentration is 0.30 osmol L−1, not 0.15.

A student who thinks water moves towards the more dilute solution, and who has also ignored dissociation, picks this. Water moves towards higher osmotic concentration, and in any case the solution is 0.30 osmol L−1, equal to plasma.

A student who thinks water moves towards the more dilute side picks this. Osmosis is net movement of water from lower to higher osmotic concentration; here the saline is 0.30 osmol L−1 once its ions are counted, equal to the cell contents and the plasma, so there is no net movement (D3.3.7).

mcqs.q: Which statement about ultrafiltration in the glomerulus is correct?
options: Only urea and other toxins pass into Bowman's capsule, while glucose is retained in the blood.
Glucose, urea and salts all pass into Bowman's capsule, but plasma proteins do not.
Water and solutes enter Bowman's capsule by osmosis and diffusion down gradients.
The filtrate is almost all excreted as urine after small changes in the tubule.
mcqs.specStatementText: Ultrafiltration, then selective reabsorption
mcqs.explain: The glomerular filter (fenestrated capillary wall, basement membrane and podocyte slits) discriminates by size only. High blood pressure forces water and all small solutes through; blood cells and plasma proteins are retained, so the filtrate is plasma minus its proteins.
rationales: A student who imagines a filter that recognizes waste picks this. Ultrafiltration is not selective for toxins; glucose passes freely and is recovered afterwards by reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule.

The glomerular filter (fenestrated capillary wall, basement membrane and podocyte slits) discriminates by size only. High blood pressure forces water and all small solutes through; blood cells and plasma proteins are retained, so the filtrate is plasma minus its proteins.

A student who assigns every membrane crossing to diffusion or osmosis picks this. The filtrate has the same small-solute concentration as plasma, so there is no gradient; filtration is bulk flow driven by blood pressure.
A student who thinks urine is essentially the filtrate picks this. About 180 litres are filtered a day and about 1.5 litres of urine are produced; the great majority of the filtrate is reabsorbed.

mcqs.q: Fluid was sampled from Bowman's capsule and from the end of the proximal convoluted tubule of a healthy kidney. Glucose was 5 mmol L−1 in the capsule and undetectable at the end of the tubule. Urea was 5 mmol L−1 in the capsule and higher at the end of the tubule. Which explanation is correct?
options: Glucose diffuses back into the blood down its own concentration gradient, whereas urea is unable to diffuse.
Urea is actively secreted into the tubule fluid, while the glucose is respired by the tubule cells.
Glucose is reabsorbed by active transport; urea is left behind and concentrates as water is reabsorbed.
The 5 mmol L−1 of glucose in the capsule shows that the glomerular filter of this kidney has been damaged.
mcqs.specStatementText: Ultrafiltration, then selective reabsorption
mcqs.explain: Tubule cells actively transport all the glucose out of the filtrate and back to the blood. Urea is not actively reabsorbed, and because most of the water leaves the tubule by osmosis the urea that remains becomes more concentrated in the smaller volume.
rationales: A student who thinks reabsorption is passive picks this. Glucose in the filtrate starts at the same concentration as in plasma, so there is no gradient for diffusion; complete recovery requires active transport by tubule cells with many mitochondria.
A student who has misassigned the transport processes picks this. Urea is not actively pumped in the proximal tubule, and the glucose is returned to the blood, not consumed by the tubule cells.

Tubule cells actively transport all the glucose out of the filtrate and back to the blood. Urea is not actively reabsorbed, and because most of the water leaves the tubule by osmosis the urea that remains becomes more concentrated in the smaller volume.

A student who believes glucose is never filtered picks this. Glucose is small enough to pass a healthy glomerular filter and appears in the filtrate at plasma concentration; its absence from urine is due to reabsorption.

mcqs.q: How does the loop of Henle make it possible for the kidney to produce concentrated urine?
options: Its ascending limb actively transports water out of the filtrate and into the tiny blood vessels of the medulla.
It absorbs sodium ions into the filtrate so that the urine leaving the loop is already highly concentrated.
Its cells actively pump water into the collecting ducts, from which the blood then reabsorbs it directly.
Its ascending limb pumps sodium ions into the medulla, so water leaves the collecting ducts by osmosis.
mcqs.specStatementText: The loop of Henle salts the medulla
mcqs.explain: Active transport of sodium ions out of the ascending limb keeps the interstitial fluid of the medulla at a high osmotic concentration. The collecting ducts pass through this medulla, so when they are permeable to water it is drawn out of them by osmosis, concentrating the urine.
rationales: A student who thinks the loop removes water directly picks this. Water is never actively transported, and the ascending limb is impermeable to water; it pumps sodium ions, and the water leaves later from the collecting ducts.

A student who has the direction of transport reversed picks this. Sodium ions are pumped out of the ascending limb into the medulla, so the fluid leaving the loop is actually dilute; the concentrating step happens in the collecting ducts.

A student who reaches for active transport to move water picks this. Water crosses the collecting duct wall by osmosis through aquaporins, driven by the high osmotic concentration the loop maintains in the medulla.

Active transport of sodium ions out of the ascending limb keeps the interstitial fluid of the medulla at a high osmotic concentration. The collecting ducts pass through this medulla, so when they are permeable to water it is drawn out of them by osmosis, concentrating the urine.

mcqs.q: In a healthy kidney the osmotic concentration of the interstitial fluid rises from 0.3 osmol L−1 in the cortex to about 1.2 osmol L−1 in the deep medulla. A drug blocks the active transport of sodium ions in the ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Which prediction is best supported?
options: The medullary gradient decays towards 0.3 osmol L−1, so less water leaves the collecting ducts and the urine becomes more dilute.
The loop can no longer reabsorb water directly, but the collecting ducts are unaffected, so the urine is unchanged.
Water reabsorption in the collecting ducts continues normally, because it is driven by pumps that ADH switches on.
Urea can no longer be excreted, so it accumulates in the blood while the volume of urine stays about the same.
mcqs.specStatementText: The loop of Henle salts the medulla
mcqs.explain: The high osmotic concentration of the medulla is maintained by sodium ions pumped out of the ascending limb. Without that pumping the gradient dissipates, the osmotic force drawing water out of the collecting ducts weakens, and a larger volume of more dilute urine is produced (this is how loop diuretics act).
rationales: The high osmotic concentration of the medulla is maintained by sodium ions pumped out of the ascending limb. Without that pumping the gradient dissipates, the osmotic force drawing water out of the collecting ducts weakens, and a larger volume of more dilute urine is produced (this is how loop diuretics act).

A student who thinks the loop's job is to remove water itself picks this. The loop's contribution is the medullary gradient; losing it does affect the collecting ducts, because there is no longer a strong osmotic gradient to draw water out of them.

A student who believes ADH activates water pumps picks this. ADH only inserts aquaporins; the driving force is osmosis into the concentrated medulla. With the gradient gone, aquaporins alone cannot move much water.

A student who merges osmoregulation with excretion picks this. Urea is removed by filtration and left in the filtrate; blocking sodium transport in the loop changes water balance, not the excretion of urea.

mcqs.q: A person has drunk very little water for a day and their blood osmotic concentration has risen. Which sequence of events follows?
options: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect the rise; the pituitary secretes less ADH, so that water is retained rather than excreted in urine.
Hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect the rise; the pituitary secretes more ADH; aquaporins move into the collecting duct membranes.
Cells in the kidney detect the rise and secrete ADH, and the collecting ducts then reabsorb more water from the filtrate.
The pituitary secretes more ADH, and ADH makes the collecting duct cells actively pump water back into the blood.
mcqs.specStatementText: ADH and aquaporins set the urine volume
mcqs.explain: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus respond to the higher osmotic concentration, the rate of ADH secretion from the pituitary gland increases, and ADH causes vesicles carrying aquaporins to fuse with the membranes of collecting duct cells. More water is reabsorbed and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced.
rationales: A student who has the direction of ADH's effect reversed picks this. ADH is anti-diuretic: more of it means more water reabsorbed. Dehydration increases, not decreases, ADH secretion.

Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus respond to the higher osmotic concentration, the rate of ADH secretion from the pituitary gland increases, and ADH causes vesicles carrying aquaporins to fuse with the membranes of collecting duct cells. More water is reabsorbed and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced.

A student who places the sensor in the organ that responds picks this. The osmoreceptors are in the hypothalamus and ADH is released from the pituitary gland; the kidney is the effector, not the detector.
A student who thinks water is pumped picks this. ADH inserts aquaporins into the membrane; water then moves by osmosis into the concentrated medulla. There is no active transport of water.

mcqs.q: After drinking a litre of water, a person produces a large volume of dilute urine within an hour. What has happened in the cells of the collecting ducts?
options: Aquaporin genes have been switched off, so no new water channels are being made for the membrane.
More ADH has been secreted, and ADH increases the volume of urine that the ducts must release.
Aquaporins have been withdrawn into vesicles, so the membrane is far less permeable to water.
The duct cells sensed the dilute blood themselves and stopped pumping water inward.
mcqs.specStatementText: ADH and aquaporins set the urine volume
mcqs.explain: The fall in blood osmotic concentration reduces osmoreceptor signalling, ADH secretion falls, and the aquaporins are removed from the collecting duct cell membranes by endocytosis into intracellular vesicles. Water can no longer leave the duct by osmosis, so dilute urine is produced.
rationales: A student who thinks the number of channels is set by protein synthesis picks this. The change within an hour is far too fast for that; aquaporins already made are shuttled between vesicles and the membrane in response to ADH.
A student who reads ADH as a diuretic picks this. ADH reduces urine volume; after drinking water its secretion falls, which is what allows the large volume of dilute urine.

The fall in blood osmotic concentration reduces osmoreceptor signalling, ADH secretion falls, and the aquaporins are removed from the collecting duct cell membranes by endocytosis into intracellular vesicles. Water can no longer leave the duct by osmosis, so dilute urine is produced.
A student who places the sensor in the kidney picks this. The osmoreceptors are in the hypothalamus; the duct cells simply respond to the fall in ADH, and water is never pumped in either direction.

mcqs.q: At wakeful rest a person's cardiac output is 5 dm3 per minute, of which skeletal muscle receives 1.0, gut 1.2, kidneys 1.1 and brain 0.75 dm3 per minute. During vigorous exercise cardiac output is 20 dm3 per minute: skeletal muscle 16, gut 0.6, kidneys 0.6 and brain 0.75 dm3 per minute. Which conclusion do these figures support?
options: Brain blood flow falls sharply, since its share of cardiac output drops from 15% to under 4%.
The kidneys receive more blood in exercise, because 0.6 is a larger part of 20 than 1.1 is of 5.
Brain blood flow rose by the same factor as cardiac output, keeping its share of the total constant.
Brain blood flow is unchanged, while gut and kidney flow fall as muscle flow rises.
mcqs.specStatementText: Blood is redirected as activity changes
mcqs.explain: The brain receives 0.75 dm3 per minute in both states. Muscle flow rises sixteen-fold and takes 80% of the enlarged output, while vasoconstriction halves the flow to the gut and kidneys. This is the redistribution of blood supply with activity.
rationales: A student who confuses share with amount picks this. The brain's percentage falls only because the total rose; the absolute flow it receives, 0.75 dm3 per minute, is exactly the same.
A student who expects the kidneys to work harder in exercise picks this, but the arithmetic is wrong: 0.6 of 20 is 3%, whereas 1.1 of 5 is 22%. Kidney flow falls in both absolute and relative terms.
A student who assumes the brain must be supplied in proportion to activity picks this. The figures show brain flow held constant at 0.75 dm3 per minute while cardiac output quadrupled.

The brain receives 0.75 dm3 per minute in both states. Muscle flow rises sixteen-fold and takes 80% of the enlarged output, while vasoconstriction halves the flow to the gut and kidneys. This is the redistribution of blood supply with activity.

mcqs.q: During sleep, cardiac output falls to about 4 dm3 per minute. Which pattern of blood supply to the organs is expected?
options: Muscle flow is minimal and brain flow is maintained, while the gut and kidneys still receive large shares.
Every organ's blood flow falls by the same fraction, because the heart is simply pumping less blood.
Brain blood flow falls to a small fraction of its waking value, since the brain itself is resting.
Kidney blood flow falls to near zero, since so little metabolic waste is produced during sleep.
mcqs.specStatementText: Blood is redirected as activity changes
mcqs.explain: With no muscular work, skeletal muscle arterioles are constricted and muscle takes little of the output. The brain's flow is held nearly constant in all states. The gut and kidneys, no longer competing with muscle, continue to receive large shares for digestion and excretion.
rationales: With no muscular work, skeletal muscle arterioles are constricted and muscle takes little of the output. The brain's flow is held nearly constant in all states. The gut and kidneys, no longer competing with muscle, continue to receive large shares for digestion and excretion.

A student who thinks cardiac output is shared out in fixed proportions picks this. Arterioles in each organ set its share, so a fall in output is not spread evenly: muscle loses most, the brain loses almost nothing.

A student who assumes brain blood flow tracks how busy the brain feels picks this. Brain flow is kept nearly constant during sleep, wakeful rest and exercise alike; the sleeping brain remains highly active.

A student who reasons from imagined need picks this. Metabolism, and so urea production, continues during sleep, and the kidneys keep receiving a large share of cardiac output; it is during vigorous exercise that their flow is cut.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic D3.3 Homeostasis

specStatements.text: Insulin and glucagon control blood glucose
Thermoregulation: sensors, control centre, hormone, effectors
The human responses to hot and cold
Excretion and osmoregulation are different jobs
The loop of Henle salts the medulla
ADH and aquaporins set the urine volume
Blood is redirected as activity changes

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Thermoregulation is treated in detail only for humans. Birds and mammals are mentioned once (c14) as the groups that regulate body temperature by physiological and behavioural means; no item tests a non-human mechanism (no countercurrent heat exchange in limbs, no panting, no torpor or hibernation, no huddling or basking as tested content).

The loop of Henle is treated only as the ascending limb pumping sodium ions into the medulla to maintain its high osmotic concentration, which lets water leave the collecting ducts by osmosis. Nothing is included on the counter-current multiplier as a quantitative mechanism, on the permeability differences of the two limbs beyond what the limit requires, on chloride co-transport, on urea recycling, or on the relative loop lengths of desert and other mammals.
